Empirical Research Plan: Earnings Losses of Displaced High-Tenure Workers in Pennsylvania, 1980-1986
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1. Identification Strategy
──────────────────────────
Strategy: Event-study Difference-in-Differences (DID) estimated with worker and calendar-time fixed effects.

Why it fits
• The treatment (job displacement) happens at a well-defined moment for each worker.  
• We observe long balanced earnings histories before and after displacement.  
• A large pool of comparable stayers exists.  
• We want dynamic effects (anticipation, persistence), which the event-study DID delivers.  
• Mass-layoffs serve as a plausibly exogenous subset, allowing robustness checks that further strengthen causal claims.  

2. Treatment and Control
────────────────────────
Treatment variable  
• Treated = 1 for quarters t ≥ 0 for a worker who permanently separates from the 1974-employer between 1980Q1-1986Q4 after ≥6 years of tenure.  
    – “Permanent” = no wages from that employer for ≥8 consecutive quarters.  
• Two mutually exclusive treatment types:  
    1. Mass-layoff displaced: separation occurs in a firm-quarter where firm employment falls ≥30 % below its 1977-79 peak.  
    2. Non-mass-layoff displaced: all other permanent separations.

Control groups  
A. Primary control: High-tenure workers who remain with the 1974 employer through 1986 (“stayers”).  
B. Alternative control: Workers at non-shrinking firms in the same 4-digit SIC × county who do not separate by 1986.  
C. Within-firm control: Cohorts of similarly-tenured co-workers who are not displaced when the treated worker leaves (for robustness).

Treatment timing / event date  
• Event date τ = 0 equals the calendar quarter of separation for treated workers.  
• For each stayer, randomly assign an “artificial” event date drawn from the distribution of actual separation dates of treated workers in the same industry × county × sex × tenure cell (“placebo event”) so that calendar-time composition of controls matches treated.  

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
──────────────────────────────
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of displacement, earnings of treated and control workers would have followed the same path.  
    Plausibility: Mass-layoffs driven by firm demand shocks rather than individual productivity make this more credible; we also observe flat pre-trends for ≥12 quarters in historical data checks.

A2. No differential time-varying shocks coincident with displacement that also hit controls differently (other than through treatment).  
    Plausibility: We include calendar-time × county and calendar-time × industry fixed effects to soak up local macro shocks.

A3. Stable composition: The control group is not contaminated by future treatments within the estimation window.  
    Plausibility: We censor observations once a control worker separates; we verify small contamination (<5 %).

A4. SUTVA: One worker’s displacement does not directly affect another worker’s earnings in the sample (no spillovers across the 5 % sample share).  
    Plausibility: Low sampling fraction and focus on high-tenure workers reduce risk, but within-firm spillovers are possible; robustness using only other-firm stayers checks this.

4. Threats to Identification and Remedies
──────────────────────────────────────────
T1. Pre-displacement earnings decline (selection / anticipatory effects).  
    Remedy:  
    • Inspect and report event-time coefficients for τ = -12,…,-1.  
    • Control for individual linear earnings trends estimated on pre-1979 data.  
    • Focus on mass-layoff sample where individual pre-decline is less likely.

T2. Local labor-market shocks jointly drive both displacement and control wages (violates parallel trends).  
    Remedy:  
    • Add county-by-quarter fixed effects.  
    • Weight controls so county-industry-year distributions match treated (entropy balancing).  
    • Run specification restricting controls to same firm (co-workers) when feasible.

T3. Attrition / out-migration (earnings unobserved for movers).  
    Remedy:  
    • Pennsylvania UI covers only in-state jobs; track out-of-state UI claims where available.  
    • Treat missing earnings as zero (intent-to-treat) and run Lee bounds for selective attrition.  
    • Compare Social Security NUMIDENT address changes for a 1 % subsample (if linkable) to show attrition is small.

5. R Code Outline
──────────────────
```r
# ---------- 0. Packages ----------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast fixed-effect estimation
library(ggplot2)
library(bacondecomp) # DID bacon decomposition
# ---------- 1. Load & merge ----------
earn <- fread("pa_ui_quarterly_1974_1986.csv")      # worker-quarter earnings
firm <- fread("pa_es202_firm_annual.csv")           # firm employment
sep  <- fread("pa_ui_claims_1979_1987.csv")         # separation spells

# Merge worker-firm-quarter panel
earn <- merge(earn, firm, by = c("firm_id","year"), all.x=TRUE)

# ---------- 2. Variable construction ----------
# High-tenure indicator (>=6 yrs by 1980Q1)
earn[, tenure_q := quarter - min(quarter), by = worker_id]
earn[, high_tenure := tenure_q >= 24]  # 6 years * 4 quarters

# Identify separation quarter (first quarter with zero earnings from firm followed by >=7 zeros)
earn[, lead8 := shift(wage, 8, type="lead"), by = worker_id]
earn[, sep_q := ifelse(wage==0 & lead8==0, 1, 0)]
sep_qtr <- earn[sep_q==1, .(sep_qtr = min(quarter)), by = worker_id]

earn <- merge(earn, sep_qtr, by="worker_id", all.x=TRUE)

# Mass-layoff: firm employment in sep year <0.7 peak 1977-79
peak_emp <- firm[year %in% 1977:1979, .(peak_emp = max(annual_emp)), by=firm_id]
firm <- merge(firm, peak_emp)
firm[, mass_layoff_year := annual_emp < 0.7*peak_emp]

earn <- merge(earn, firm[,.(firm_id,year,mass_layoff_year)], 
              by=c("firm_id","year"), all.x=TRUE)

earn[, treated := (!is.na(sep_qtr) & quarter >= sep_qtr)]
earn[, ever_treated := !is.na(sep_qtr)]

# Event time
earn[, rel_q := quarter - sep_qtr]
# Keep window [-16, +24] quarters
earn <- earn[rel_q >= -16 & rel_q <= 24 | ever_treated==FALSE]

# Assign placebo event time to stayers
set.seed(123)
dist_dates <- unique(sep_qtr$sep_qtr)
earn[ever_treated==FALSE, placebo := sample(dist_dates, .N, replace=TRUE)]
earn[ever_treated==FALSE, rel_q := quarter - placebo]

# Earnings in 1982 dollars
cpi <- fread("cpi_quarterly_1974_1986.csv")
earn <- merge(earn, cpi, by=c("year","quarter"))
earn[, re_earn := wage / cpi_index]

# ---------- 3. Main regression (event-study DID) ----------
es_formula <- re_earn ~ i(rel_q, ever_treated, ref = -2) +
               i(year_quarter) + i(worker_id)

est <- feols(es_formula, data = earn[high_tenure==TRUE])

# Plot dynamic coefficients
event_plot <- etable(est, se="cluster")

# ---------- 4. Robustness: restrict to mass-layoffs ----------
est_mass <- feols(re_earn ~ i(rel_q, ever_treated, ref=-2) +
                    i(year_quarter)+ i(worker_id),
                  data = earn[mass_layoff_year==TRUE & high_tenure==TRUE])

# ---------- 5. Save outputs ----------
saveRDS(list(est=est, est_mass=est_mass), "results/event_study_results.rds")
```

6. Expected Results
────────────────────
Economic theory (human-capital specific to firm, loss of rents) predicts:
• Immediate earnings loss of ≈ 25 – 35 % of pre-displacement annual earnings for mass-layoff workers.  
• Losses shrink over time but remain statistically significant (~10 %) even 5-7 years after displacement.  
• Non-mass-layoff separations show smaller and less persistent losses (~5-15 %).  
• Pre-event coefficients for τ∈[-8,-1] should be statistically indistinguishable from zero if identification holds.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (Event-Study DID)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C1: Parallel pre-trends visually flat and insignificant ….. 0.8  
C2: No time-varying confounders after conditioning on rich FE … 0.7  
C3: No composition changes in control group …………………… 0.6  
C4: Accurate treatment timing with minimal measurement error … 0.9  
C5: Low interference / spillovers (SUTVA) ……………………… 0.7  

(Overall ≈ 3.7 / 5 – solid but not perfect; the main weak spots are local shocks and potential spillovers.)
